prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical discovery of the Z2 topological insulator and quantum spin Hall state, and its experimental realisation in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: Topological insulators remain, for me, the deepest conceptual step on the list. The Kane-Mele Z2 classification showed that time-reversal-invariant band insulators fall into distinct topological classes, with spin-orbit coupling producing protected boundary states, and Molenkamp's HgTe quantum-well transport experiment confirmed this in a clean and unambiguous way. The idea has since spread through ARPES, transport, photonics and the search for Majorana modes, and it has been reproduced independently for almost two decades. It is a theory-plus-decisive-experiment structure that fits the Nobel pattern well. Seven of eight colleagues placed it in their top three, which I do not count as merit in itself, but it does tell me the scientific case is not an idiosyncrasy of my own ranking. After reading the ballots I have changed my proposed trio from Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan to Kane, Mele and Molenkamp.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. Any three-person cut leaves out real contributors: Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang (who proposed HgTe, and Zhang is deceased), Fu, Moore and Balents for the three-dimensional theory, and Hasan and collaborators for the first 3D observations. Choosing Kane, Mele and Molenkamp gives the cleanest 2D theory-plus-experiment story but leaves the 3D materials discovery uncredited in the citation. There is also a legitimate question of how far the 2016 prize for topological phase transitions and phases already covered this ground, and whether the committee would prefer a candidate with a more clearly separate subject.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks twisted bilayer graphene first, as a rare case where a band-structure prediction led directly to a new experimental field, and ranks topological insulators second while including Mele and leaving out Hasan. He also notes that the 2016 topological prize might count against B006.
responses.response: I agree with Eriksson on Mele and now follow him. Kane and Mele wrote the founding Z2 papers together, and omitting Mele cannot be justified by the three-person limit when the 3D credit is already diffuse. On the 2016 overlap I disagree: that prize rewarded topological phase transitions, Chern-type invariants from broken time reversal and 1D chains. The Z2 invariant with time-reversal symmetry and spin-orbit coupling is a distinct discovery with a distinct experimental realisation. On B017 I respect the clean Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction followed by experiment, but I still think the unresolved superconducting mechanism makes it a year or two early compared with B006, so I keep it as my first alternative.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks B006 first with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, notes that Hasan's 3D ARPES work is a further claim, and sees the omitted names as a real attribution problem.
responses.response: This was the most persuasive argument for changing my own trio. My opening ballot favoured Hasan to represent the 3D materials discovery, but the 3D theory is shared by Fu, Kane and Mele, Moore and Balents, and the first observations involved competing materials and priority questions, so any single experimental name is contestable. The 2D theory plus HgTe experiment is the more defensible and compact core. I accept that this leaves Hasan out and I flag that as the main weakness, but I do not think naming him is worth the cost of dropping Mele.

responses.point: Olsson ranks B006 first with Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan, arguing for a theory-plus-two-experiments balance and acknowledging that leaving Mele out is a real allocation cost.
responses.response: Olsson and I opened with the same trio and made the same argument, so I owe a reason for moving. The balance of one theorist and two experimentalists is attractive, but it rests on treating the Bi-Sb and Bi2Se3 ARPES results as the single decisive 3D experiment, and that is exactly where I now see the weakest consensus. I would rather credit both theorists of the foundational paper with the first experimental observation than split the theory credit. I recognise that Olsson's configuration is still reasonable and would support it if the committee finds Mele's omission less costly than I now do.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first, as a conceptually clean transfer of cavity QED to superconducting circuits that is distinct from the 2025 prize, while discounting his own enthusiasm as someone who works in the area.
responses.response: I take the declaration of interest seriously and I find cQED a strong candidate, which is why I list it as my second alternative. Where I differ is on the character of the contribution. Dispersive readout and strong coupling on a chip are extraordinarily important, but I read them as an enabling architecture whose largest consequences lie in quantum technology, whereas the Z2 invariant is a new classification of matter. The 2025 prize for macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits also sits very close, and I think an award in the same community within a year would need a strong argument for distinctness. Girvin's omission from the credited names is an additional attribution gap for B038.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks first as the most compelling case from an atomic-physics and measurement viewpoint, with a clean two-person credit, while acknowledging that the 2005 and 2012 prizes are adjacent.
responses.response: I accept that B047 has the cleanest attribution of anything on the shortlist and that the precision, geodesy and fundamental-constants payoff is real. Clocks did not appear in my top four, and I want to be open that this reflects my own field distance as a string theorist rather than a verdict against it. My reservation is the one Kroll names: the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes cover much of the underlying toolbox, and the step to the lattice clock is a refinement of accuracy rather than a new kind of phenomenon. I would be reassured if colleagues in atomic physics argue convincingly that the magic-wavelength idea is a distinct conceptual invention, since that is the crux.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept omitting Hasan and the HgTe proposers (Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang) in a Kane, Mele and Molenkamp trio, and whether an alternative such as two parts could improve fairness without exceeding three people.
Whether the 2016 prize is judged to leave enough room for a second topological-matter award.
Whether the unresolved superconducting mechanism in magic-angle graphene should delay B017, or whether the discovery of the phases and the flat band is sufficient.
How much weight a second superconducting-circuit prize so soon after 2025 should carry against cQED's undeniable impact.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile. My documented connections are my PhD supervisor David Gross, my early mentor Hector Rubinstein, my co-author Thomas Van Riet and the Uppsala theory group, none of whom is a credited name on any shortlisted candidate. My own research is in string theory and cosmology, so I am an outsider to every shortlisted subject and defer to specialists on technical details.
